sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Consequentialism
sources.use: Sections 1, 2, and 5: direct act criterion, maximizing requirement, and act-versus-rule distinction.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only. Neither question has an empirically validated interpretation.
sources.claim: Act consequentialism applies the moral-rightness criterion directly to an act’s own consequences; in its maximizing form, an act is right only when its outcome is at least as good as the outcomes of available alternatives. This differs from full rule consequentialism, which makes wrongness depend on consequence-justified rules (sections 1, 2, and 5).

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Rule Consequentialism
sources.use: Sections 4 and 8: rule-based criterion of wrongness, act-versus-rule distinction, and the separate decision-procedure issue.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only. Neither question has an empirically validated interpretation.
sources.claim: For a full rule-consequentialist criterion of wrongness, acts are wrong when forbidden by rules justified by their consequences. This differs from using consequence-justified rules merely as a decision procedure while direct act outcomes determine wrongness (sections 4 and 8).

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Moral Cognitivism vs. Non-Cognitivism
sources.use: Introduction and sections 1.1–1.3, 2.3, and 5: truth-aptness, belief expression, cognitivist subjectivism, and minimalist/quasi-realist limits.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only; neither original question is empirically validated.
sources.claim: Cognitivist accounts treat ordinary moral sentences as truth-apt and their acceptance as belief-like. Noncognitivist accounts question substantial truth conditions or belief expression, although sophisticated expressivists may allow deflationary truth talk. Truth-aptness alone does not establish that any moral claim is true.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Theory and Observation in Science
sources.use: Section 2.1: intersubjectively ascertainable observation reports and publicly appraisable theory tests; sections 1–2 discuss theory-ladenness and the limits of simple objectivity.
sources.reuse: Conceptual distinction only; original Worldview Sorter questions are not validated by this source.
sources.claim: Intersubjectively ascertainable observations and public theory testing are a recognized rationale for the epistemic credibility of empirical claims; the account also acknowledges theory-ladenness and does not make every private experience worthless.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Arguments for Incompatibilism
sources.use: Introduction and section 1 distinguish the free-will compatibility conditional from actual determinism, moral responsibility, fatalism, and mere causation.
sources.claim: The free-will incompatibilist denies that a choice fixed by the complete prior state and laws can be free; this conditional does not assert that determinism is actually true or settle moral responsibility.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only; neither original question nor its evidence threshold is empirically validated.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Compatibilism
sources.use: The distinct alternative-possibilities and sourcehood discussions delimit the conditional and reasons-based compatibilist alternatives.
sources.claim: Compatibilist theories can allow free choice under determinism, while the alternatives-possibilities and sourcehood debates do not collapse into a single necessary condition.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only; neither original question nor its evidence threshold is empirically validated.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Religious Experience
sources.use: Section 3 contrasts defeasible first-person experiential reasons with objections to the evidential value of religious experience.
sources.claim: A recognized account permits an apparent religious experience to give its subject defeasible initial grounds for a factual belief without independent verification; the subject's grounds and an outsider's testimonial grounds are distinct and disputed.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only; neither original question nor its evidence threshold is empirically validated.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Divine Revelation
sources.use: Provides context for the epistemic status of putative divine revelation and distinctions among experiential, inferential, and testimonial accounts.
sources.claim: The epistemic status of putative revelation is disputed; revelation as an apparent communication is distinct from the truth of its content and from its authority for outsiders.
sources.reuse: Conceptual basis only; neither original question nor its evidence threshold is empirically validated.
